title: Europe’s Bomb Threats Raise Fears of Hybrid Warfare
author: Rebecca Schneid
body:
A wave of bomb threats this week targeted dozens of flights across Europe before expanding to include newsrooms, leaving authorities scrambling to find those responsible. The bomb threats—all since identified as hoaxes—came through almost daily via anonymous calls and emails beginning Nov. 2.

On Monday, a Wizz Air flight traveling from London to Bulgaria was diverted after a bomb threat was received mid-flight, making an emergency landing in Budapest. At least seven passenger flights were targeted the following day, which led to emergency landings, searches, and diversions. More than two dozen additional flights were targeted Thursday, and threats continued into Friday.

Affected flights connected countries including Italy, Ireland, Spain, Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, Finland, Austria, Denmark, Belgium, Portugal, France, Greece, Serbia, Czechia, and the United Kingdom.

Authorities, including the U.K. Transport Secretary, have since described them as “hoaxes,” as no attacks were carried out and each affected flight was landed safely. But the hoaxes were not harmless; they affected thousands of people’s flight plans, struck fear into potential travelers, and impacted the carefully structured aviation ecosystem.

The malicious efforts expanded Friday when a warning was sent by email to several European broadcasters claiming that bombs had been planted in their buildings, forcing evacuations at outlets like Sky News, Bulgaria’s Nova TV, and Irish public broadcaster RTÉ.

“What happened this week is just a small part of what awaits Europe in the near future,” the message sent to broadcasters said, according to Reuters.

European Union Transport Commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas strongly condemned the threats on X on Friday, saying that he has activated EU-level aviation security information-sharing mechanisms. He added that it was “too early” to draw conclusions on whether the hoaxes were linked.

Ireland’s government, meanwhile, said Friday that “it seems likely that this is a co-ordinated campaign of disruption.”

Experts tell TIME that the threats themselves might be the point—launching a fear campaign meant to disrupt systems and put millions of people on edge.

Could the bomb threats be hybrid warfare?

Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares told Spanish broadcast news on Friday that the threats were an “attempt at hybrid aggression and psychological warfare.”

Elisabeth Braw, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, which is a nonpartisan think tank for global affairs based in D.C., says that these kinds of threats fall into what she calls “gray zone conflicts,” meaning that they’re “in the gray zone between war and peace.”

For example, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni told an Italian news station on Friday that “what’s being attacked is civilian infrastructure,” rather than military or weapons infrastructure. This puts European nations in a tight spot, Braw says, especially if the actor is another nation.

“If you attack another country's military, that country's military will strike back. That is the nature of war,” she explains. “Whereas if you target civilian infrastructure, what is that country going to do? It’s not going to respond with military means, simply because then you would have war.”

Bomb threats against airliners are not new, Braw says, but their scale and frequency this week stand out.

“What is concerning this time is it's such a significant number, and the fact that these have come in such close succession, and it comes against the background of all these other attacks and really geopolitically motivated crimes targeting European countries,” Braw adds, referencing another destabilization operation that recently hit Europe.

Cyberattacks targeted refrigeration systems at grocery stores in at least nine countries across Europe and at blood banks in France, following similar attacks on French supermarkets in mid-October.

Two pro-Russian hacktivist groups claimed responsibility for the cyberattack campaign on supermarkets Wednesday, though their involvement remains unconfirmed.

U.S. federal agencies released a fact sheet the following day that called on hospitals, transportation systems, and food retailers to “defend against this activity by using strong authentication.”

Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov distanced the Russian government from the cyberattacks on Thursday, calling any allegations “absurd” and “unfounded.”

Robert Jordan, a program director at the Royal United Services Institute, tells TIME that it might be “tempting” to ascribe the threats to hostile states like Russia.

“Certainly there are well-founded instances of Russian and Iranian groups recruiting people online using secure communications applications to conduct similar activity,” he says.

At the same time, he continues, there is no way yet to discount that this is an individual or non-state-affiliated group exploiting safety standards in the region to “cause chaos.”

Before the parties responsible can be ascertained, or their motives investigated, security personnel must identify where these threats are originating from, he says.

Until they do, disruptions to airports are likely to continue, Jordan says. Even suspected hoaxes demand serious consideration, Braw adds, given the potentially devastating consequences of a real attack.

“You have to take every threat seriously in the sector, but especially in aviation, where the consequences would be so utterly devastating if an incident were successful, and so that's why we have seen all these airliners making emergency landings,” she says. “All of that causes disruption and it causes anxiety among passengers, and it also causes significant financial costs and losses for the airlines.”

French prosecutors are investigating whether foreign powers are connected to the bomb threats, Agence France-Presse (AFP) reported Saturday. The purpose of the investigation is to find “the authors of the emails who disseminated this false information ... and to determine any potential links they may have to foreign powers,” the Paris prosecutor’s office is quoted as saying.

Some of the emails were signed "fighters of the Male State," which matches the name of a radical misogynist group in Russia, though there has been no confirmed link, according to AFP. The group's founder, Vladislav Pozdniakov, denied any involvement, saying on social media Friday that the "movement does not exist since 2021."

“Identifying who is doing this will rapidly be escalating up the priority ladder for law enforcement and security services across Europe,” Jordan says. “In the meantime, it is likely that airlines and airports will be meeting to determine how much extra screening scrutiny the system can bear.”

Even after learning who made the bomb threats, European nations might not be any closer to knowing how to respond to similar hybrid attacks in the future, Braw says.

“As a law-abiding democracy, you can't say, ‘Well, if they threaten our airlines, we will threaten them.’ That’s not how democracies operate,” Braw says. “Yet you can't allow these sorts of activities to continue to proliferate, and that is a dilemma for European governments every single day these days.”

The dilemma is becoming more and more “acute,” she adds, as the threats accelerate and grow more sophisticated.
